5.10.8 Seller Onboarding Workflow

Seller onboarding is the gateway through which new Business Owners gain full access to the Talentree platform. The workflow begins during account registration: when a user registers with the *BusinessOwner* role, a corresponding BusinessOwnerProfile entity is automatically created with an *Approved* initial status (configurable) and linked to the AppUser identity record.

In the manual review variant of the workflow, the administrator uses the AdminService methods ApproveBusinessOwnerAsync and RejectBusinessOwnerAsync to act on pending applications. Upon approval, the following events occur atomically:

* The BusinessOwnerProfile.Status is set to *Approved*, with the approving admin's identity and timestamp recorded.  
* A welcome email containing dashboard access information is dispatched through EmailService.  
* An in-platform notification is created via NotificationHelperService.NotifyBusinessOwnerApproved().  
* An audit log entry is written through AuditLogService for compliance.

Rejection follows the same pattern but records the mandatory RejectionReason on the profile entity and dispatches a rejection email with the stated reason.

5.10.9 Homepage Content Management

The HomepageManagementService gives platform administrators granular control over all curated content displayed on the Talentree customer-facing homepage. It manages four distinct content areas: *Hero and Promotional Banners*, *Featured Brands*, *Featured Products*, and the *Announcement Bar*.

All four content types support scheduling: each entity carries optional ScheduleStart and ScheduleEnd timestamps. The GetHomepagePreviewAsync() method filters all content against the current UTC timestamp before composing the response, ensuring that scheduled promotions activate and expire automatically without any manual intervention. The system caps featured brands at ten entries and featured products at twenty, enforced at the service layer.

Banner ordering is managed through a DisplayOrder integer field. The ReorderBannersAsync() method accepts a batch of {Id, NewDisplayOrder} pairs, allowing the frontend to implement drag-and-drop reordering that is committed to the database in a single request.

5.11 Exception Handling & Logging

5.11.1 Global Exception Middleware

Talentree implements a centralized **Global Exception Handling Middleware** (`GlobalExceptionHandlingMiddleware`) registered early in the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline via `app.UseGlobalExceptionHandling()`. This middleware wraps every incoming HTTP request in a try-catch block, intercepting all unhandled exceptions before they propagate to the client as raw 500 Internal Server Error responses. This eliminates scattered try-catch blocks in controllers and enforces consistent error formatting across the entire API surface.

The middleware maps each application-defined exception type to the appropriate HTTP status code and response format using a C\# pattern-matching switch expression. Custom exception types are defined in the `Talentree.Core.Exceptions` namespace and include: `NotFoundException` (404), `BadRequestException` (400), `UnauthorizedException` (401), `ForbiddenException` (403), and `ValidationException` (400 with field-level errors). Any uncaught exception falls through to a generic 500 response with a safe error message.

A secondary security feature is embedded directly in the middleware: any **Unauthorized or Forbidden** access attempt targeting an `/admin` route is automatically recorded to the `UserActionLog` audit table via `IAuditLogService`, providing a comprehensive security event trail without requiring individual controllers to implement this logic.

*Listing 5.13 — Pattern-matched exception-to-HTTP-status-code mapping in GlobalExceptionHandlingMiddleware* 

5.11.2 Logging System

Talentree uses **Microsoft.Extensions.Logging** — ASP.NET Core's built-in structured logging abstraction — throughout the entire application. Logger instances are injected via constructor DI (`ILogger<T>`) into all services, controllers, middleware, and background consumers. In development, logs stream to the console with detailed formatting. In production on Azure App Service, logs are routed to **Azure Application Insights**, enabling centralized monitoring, alerting, and distributed trace correlation.

The logging strategy applies different levels purposefully: `LogInformation` records normal business events (user login, order created, payment processed); `LogWarning` captures suspicious events (Stripe signature failures, failed login attempts, unauthorized access); and `LogError` captures unhandled exceptions and integration failures (AI service timeout, webhook processing errors). The global middleware always calls `LogError` for every unhandled exception before generating the client response.

5.11.3 Error Response Standardization

Every API response — whether successful or error — is wrapped in the `ApiResponse<T>` generic envelope class. This ensures the frontend client can always rely on the same JSON shape regardless of the endpoint, eliminating custom parsing logic for different error formats. Table 5.16 documents the standard response structure used across all endpoints.

5.12 Backend Security

5.12.1 HTTPS & Secure Communication

All traffic to the Talentree API is encrypted using **TLS 1.2 / TLS 1.3**. In the ASP.NET Core pipeline, `app.UseHttpsRedirection()` middleware automatically redirects any incoming HTTP requests to HTTPS. On Azure App Service, TLS termination is handled at the **Azure Application Gateway / Front Door** level, ensuring end-to-end encryption between client browsers and the backend. All sensitive configuration values (JWT secret key, Stripe API keys, database connection strings, SMTP credentials, RabbitMQ URI) are stored as **Azure App Service Environment Variables** and never committed to source control.

5.12.2 SQL Injection Prevention

Talentree is protected against SQL injection through its exclusive use of **Entity Framework Core** with parameterized queries. EF Core translates all LINQ expressions into parameterized SQL statements, where user-supplied values are always bound as SQL parameters — never interpolated directly into query strings. This eliminates the entire class of SQL injection vulnerabilities at the ORM level. No raw SQL strings (`FromSqlRaw`) are used in the codebase; all data access flows through typed LINQ specifications in the `GenericRepository<T>`.

5.12.3 XSS Protection

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) prevention is achieved through multiple complementary layers: ASP.NET Core's built-in **HTML encoding** for any values rendered in views, **JSON serialization** (System.Text.Json) which escapes HTML special characters by default, and **Angular's built-in DOM sanitization** on the frontend. Additionally, the API returns only typed DTOs rather than raw entity objects, preventing accidental exposure of unsafe string content.

5.12.4 Input Validation

Talentree uses **FluentValidation** for all incoming DTO validation, registered globally via `AddFluentValidationAutoValidation()`. This applies validation rules automatically before the action method is called, with invalid requests rejected at the model binding stage and the error details returned via the standardized `ValidationException` path in the global exception middleware. Validators are co-located with their corresponding DTOs in the `Talentree.Service/Validators/` directory and cover all authentication, product, order, payout, and user management input objects.

Additional server-side protection includes: **Rate Limiting** on AI proxy endpoints (20 requests/minute per the `AdminAi` fixed-window policy), **role authorization** on every non-public endpoint, and **account lockout** after configurable consecutive failed login attempts enforced by `SecuritySettings`.

5.12.5 CORS Configuration

The Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy is configured with an **explicit allow-list** of trusted frontend origins. Only the production frontend deployments on Netlify and Vercel are permitted: `https://talentree-platform.netlify.app` and `https://talentree-platform.vercel.app`. `AllowAnyHeader()` and `AllowAnyMethod()` are combined with `AllowCredentials()` — the latter is required for SignalR WebSocket connections which attach JWT tokens as query parameters. Wildcard (`*`) origins are explicitly not used.

Table 5.18 — Backend Security Controls Summary

5.13 Media & File Management

File and image handling is a core backend infrastructure concern in Talentree. Rather than depending on a third-party CDN service such as Cloudinary, the current implementation uses **local filesystem storage** within the ASP.NET Core application's wwwroot/uploads directory. This deliberate architectural decision simplifies the development and staging environment while allowing a future cloud migration with minimal service-layer changes, since all file operations are abstracted behind the IImageService and IFileService interfaces.

5.13.1 File Upload Architecture

The upload infrastructure is divided into two complementary services, each scoped to a distinct file category. Figure 5.3 illustrates the relationship between the callers and the two services.

*Figure 5.3 — Two-Service File Upload Architecture*

**ImageService** is dedicated to image uploads consumed by product listings, knowledge-article thumbnails, and brand profile pictures. It is configured via appsettings.json under the ImageStorage key, which specifies the local filesystem base path and the public URL base. This clean separation means the configuration—and a future migration to Azure Blob Storage or AWS S3—requires changes only in the configuration and the service implementation, with zero impact on callers.

**FileService** handles general-purpose file uploads, primarily support-ticket attachments and knowledge-article downloadable resources. It resolves the physical path using IWebHostEnvironment.WebRootPath, ensuring compatibility with the ASP.NET Core hosting model.

5.13.2 Image Validation & Storage

Before any image reaches the filesystem, the ImageService.IsValidImage() method applies two guards. First, the file size is compared against the 5 MB ceiling. Second, the MIME type is checked against the allowlist { image/jpeg, image/png, image/jpg }. Both checks operate on the server-side metadata provided by the multipart upload, not on the client-supplied filename extension, mitigating common bypass attempts.

Listing 5.1 presents the core validation and upload logic extracted from the ImageService implementation.

*Listing 5.1 — ImageService: Validation and Upload Logic (ImageService.cs)*

Upon a successful upload, the service returns the relative public URL (e.g., /uploads/products/a1b2c3d4.jpg), which is persisted in the ProductImage.ImageUrl column. ASP.NET Core's static-file middleware serves these URLs directly without any additional controller involvement, keeping the read path entirely out of the application server.

For support ticket and general file attachments, the FileService applies a broader 10 MB limit and allows JPEG, PNG, GIF, PDF, and plain text files. Allowed MIME types are validated at the controller layer within SupportService.CreateTicketAsync() before FileService.UploadFileAsync() is called.

5.13.3 File Naming Strategy & Security

Both services employ a **GUID-based file naming strategy** that eliminates several classes of common web vulnerabilities. Table 5.13 compares the naming conventions of ImageService and FileService.

Table 5.13 — File Naming Conventions

The security implications of this design are significant:

* **Path Traversal Prevention:** Because the stored filename is derived from a server-generated GUID and never directly from the client-supplied name, attackers cannot craft filenames containing directory traversal sequences (e.g., ../../etc/passwd).  
* **Enumeration Resistance:** GUID-based names are practically unguessable, preventing adversaries from enumerating uploaded resources by iterating predictable names.  
* **Collision Avoidance:** The statistical uniqueness of UUID v4 eliminates accidental file overwrites even under high concurrent upload load.  
* **Extension Preservation:** ImageService preserves only the file extension from the original name (via Path.GetExtension()), while FileService retains the sanitised original name for human-readability in support contexts.

Deletion is implemented through the ImageService.DeleteImageAsync() method, which translates the stored relative URL back to a physical filesystem path using the configured base mappings and then calls File.Delete(). This ensures that orphaned image files are cleaned up when a product update removes an image or when an article is deleted. The method is designed to be idempotent: if the file does not exist on disk, the method returns silently without raising an exception.

The storage topology is organised by content category through the folder parameter passed to both services. Table 5.14 lists the folders in use across the platform.

Table 5.14 — Upload Folder Structure

Future Migration Path

While the current implementation uses local filesystem storage, the architecture is deliberately designed for cloud migration. Both `IImageService` and `IFileService` are registered via .NET Dependency Injection. Migrating to Azure Blob Storage, AWS S3, or Cloudinary would require only a new concrete implementation of these interfaces registered in the DI container—no changes to the service layer callers (`ProductService`, `SupportService`, etc.) would be needed. Configuration values such as `ImageStorage:LocalPath` and `ImageStorage:BaseUrl` can be replaced with cloud connection strings without recompilation.

5.14 API Documentation with Swagger

Talentree integrates **Swashbuckle (Swagger / OpenAPI 3.0)** for automatic API documentation generation. The Swagger UI is accessible at `/swagger` and provides an interactive interface for exploring and testing all API endpoints. The Swagger configuration is registered in `Program.cs` via `AddSwaggerGen()` with a **JWT Bearer security definition**, allowing developers to authenticate directly from the Swagger UI by pasting a JWT token — Swagger automatically prepends the `Bearer` prefix to all authenticated requests.

All controllers and action methods use `[ProducesResponseType]` attributes with the `ApiResponse<T>` wrapper type, ensuring Swagger generates accurate response schema documentation. XML documentation comments (`/// <summary>`) on controllers and action methods are reflected in the Swagger UI as human-readable endpoint descriptions, providing the development team with self-documenting API reference documentation without maintaining a separate documentation project.

Table 5.19 — Swagger/OpenAPI Documentation Coverage 

5.13 Backend Deployment & Hosting

The Talentree backend is deployed on **Microsoft Azure App Service** (PaaS), providing managed infrastructure, automatic scaling, and built-in CI/CD integration. The deployment architecture uses separate environments: the `staging` branch triggers deployment to the Azure staging slot, while `main` triggers production deployment. This branch-based deployment model ensures that all changes are validated on staging before being promoted to production via Azure's deployment slot swap feature.

5.14 Backend Technology Justification

The selection of the Talentree backend technology stack was the result of a deliberate evaluation process comparing multiple alternatives across performance, ecosystem maturity, team expertise, and alignment with the platform's scalability requirements. The following subsections document the rationale for each core technology decision.

5.14.1 Why ASP.NET Core

**ASP.NET Core 8.0** was selected as the web framework for Talentree based on its industry-leading performance benchmarks (consistently ranking in the top tier of *TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks*), its mature enterprise ecosystem, and its deep integration with Microsoft Azure — the chosen cloud platform. ASP.NET Core's built-in dependency injection, middleware pipeline, and native Identity framework significantly reduced boilerplate compared to alternatives, accelerating feature development.

5.14.2 Why SQL Server

**Microsoft SQL Server** (via Azure SQL Database) was chosen for its ACID compliance, robust support for complex relational schemas with multiple foreign key relationships, and native integration with EF Core. Azure SQL Database provides enterprise-grade high availability (99.99% SLA), automated backups, and seamless elasticity — all without infrastructure management overhead.

5.14.3 Why Entity Framework Core

**Entity Framework Core 8** was selected as the ORM for its Code-First workflow, strong LINQ query capabilities, automatic migration generation, and the Specification Pattern support it enables. EF Core's interceptors (used for the AuditInterceptor), global query filters (used for soft-delete), and configuration API (used for all entity configurations) provided enterprise-grade features with minimal code overhead.

5.14.4 Why Onion Architecture

**Onion Architecture** was selected over traditional layered (N-Tier) or flat architectures to achieve strict separation of concerns and dependency inversion. By placing the domain model (entities, interfaces, specifications) at the center with no external dependencies, the architecture guarantees that business rules are not contaminated by infrastructure concerns. The outer layers (Repository, Service, API) depend inward through abstractions, making every component independently testable and swappable.

5.15 Summary

This chapter has presented a comprehensive technical overview of the Talentree backend system, detailing the architectural decisions, implementation patterns, and technology choices that collectively form the platform's server-side foundation. The backend is built with **ASP.NET Core 8.0** following **Onion Architecture** principles, ensuring a clean, testable, and maintainable codebase organized across four project layers: Core, Repository, Service, and API.

The **database layer** (Section 5.5) employs SQL Server with EF Core Code-First migrations, hosting 56 tables across eight functional domains with global soft-delete filtering, immutable audit logs, and SuperAdmin protection enforced at the DbContext level. The **data access layer** (Section 5.6) uses the Generic Repository and Unit of Work patterns with the Specification Pattern, providing a type-safe, LINQ-powered query abstraction that supports filtering, eager loading, sorting, and pagination without EF Core logic leaking into the service layer.

**Authentication and authorization** (Section 5.7) are implemented through JWT bearer tokens with strict validation, refresh token rotation, and role-based access control across five distinct user roles. **Real-time communication** (Section 5.8) is delivered via ASP.NET Core SignalR, enabling targeted push notifications, unread count updates, and order status changes to connected users without polling.

The **Stripe payment integration** (Section 5.9) implements the PaymentIntent model with server-side intent creation, frontend card confirmation, and webhook-driven payment acknowledgment — protected by HMAC signature verification and idempotent event processing. **Cross-cutting concerns** (Sections 5.10–5.12) are handled centrally: global exception middleware maps all exception types to standardized `ApiResponse<T>` envelopes, FluentValidation enforces input integrity, and Swagger provides a live, interactive API documentation surface.

The backend is **deployed to Azure App Service** (Section 5.13) with a branch-based CI/CD pipeline, connecting to Azure SQL Database, RabbitMQ for asynchronous AI training events, and an AI microservice on Azure VM. All sensitive configuration is stored in Azure environment variables with no secrets in source control.

### **7.2 Recommendation & Personalization System** 

**\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_**

The Talentree platform incorporates a production-grade, highly-decoupled recommendation system that serves as a core AI microservice. To support both ends of our digital marketplace, the system architecture is divided into two completely independent pipelines: one serving B2C customer product personalization and another dedicated to B2B business owner procurement planning. This separation ensures that the distinct behavioral patterns of end consumers and business owners are modeled accurately without interference.

Our architectural philosophy prioritizes a decoupled feature layer. The machine learning recommendation logic is schema-independent, integrating seamlessly with standard transactional databases like Azure SQL. We employ continuous hot-reload retraining mechanisms that run in the background. This allows our FastAPI serving layers to maintain high-performance API delivery uninterrupted, promoting new candidate models to production only after they surpass rigorous validation metric gating checks.

##### **7.5.3.1 Churn Risk and Fraud Detection**

Both supervised models employ eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) \[2\] classifiers. The churn model is trained on 476 samples produced by applying a sliding time-window strategy and Gaussian noise augmentation to the nine active Business Owners in the production database. The fraud model addresses class imbalance — whereby only 8 percent of production requests carry a fraud label — by oversampling the minority class to approximately 40 percent of the training corpus. 

##### **7.5.3.2 Anomaly Detection**

Transaction anomaly detection uses the Isolation Forest algorithm \[3\], an unsupervised ensemble method trained on 1,012 historical transaction records. No labelled data is required; the model flags statistically deviant observations at inference time.

##### **7.5.3.3 Remaining Models**

Sentiment analysis employs the Valence Aware Dictionary and Sentiment Reasoner (VADER) \[4\] NLP engine. Support ticket triage applies a keyword and rule-based classifier. Demand forecasting uses Linear Regression on per-product historical quantities. Profile completeness and description quality are computed deterministically. Table 4.2 provides a full comparison across all eight deployed models.

#### **7.5.5 Database Connection**

The service connects to the production SQL Server database using SQLAlchemy's `creator` pattern rather than a standard connection URI. This is required because the database password contains special characters — including `+`, `#`, and `=` — that are misinterpreted by the ODBC parser when embedded in a URI string. As shown in Listing 4.1, the `creator` argument passes a raw pyodbc connection directly to the SQLAlchemy engine, bypassing URI encoding entirely. 

![][image43]

#### **7.5.6 Automated Scheduler**

Nine background jobs are executed automatically via APScheduler \[5\]. Eight nightly jobs run between 02:00 and 02:45 Cairo time (EET, UTC+3), covering the full prediction and compute pipeline for all active database records. One weekly job runs every Sunday at 03:00 EET to retrain all supervised machine learning models on accumulated production data. The full schedule is presented in Figure 7.5.7 and Table 7.5.4. 

![][image44]  
*Figure 7.5.7 — Execution timeline of all automated scheduler jobs. Nightly jobs span 02:00–02:45 EET; the weekly retraining job runs at 03:00 EET every Sunday.*

![][image45]

#### **7.5.7 Deployment and Continuous Integration**

The BO Dashboard AI Service is deployed on a Microsoft Azure Virtual Machine (VM) \[6\] running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The application is served using Gunicorn as the process manager with Uvicorn workers handling asynchronous HTTP traffic. All environment variables — including database credentials — are configured directly on the VM, ensuring that no secrets are stored in the source code repository.

Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) is managed through a GitHub Actions \[7\] workflow defined in .github/workflows/azure-webapp.yml. The workflow is triggered on every push to the feature/bo-dashboard branch. It executes two sequential jobs: a *build* job that installs dependencies and packages the application into a ZIP archive, and a *deploy* job that transfers the artefact to the Azure VM. As shown in Listing 7.5.2, the production startup command launches four Uvicorn workers under Gunicorn supervision.

![][image46]  
*Listing 7.5.2 — Production startup command configuring Gunicorn with four Uvicorn workers on the Azure VM.*   
The live service is accessible at [http://20.244.32.232:8000](http://20.244.32.232:8000/), with a health check endpoint at GET /ai/status that returns the service name and version. Interactive API documentation is auto-generated by FastAPI and accessible at the /docs path.

This chapter has presented the design and implementation of the BO Dashboard AI Service. The service deploys eight machine learning and rule-based models, exposes twenty-three REST endpoints, and executes nine automated background jobs on nightly and weekly schedules. The system is deployed on an Azure Virtual Machine and managed through a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline. Chapter 5 presents the Angular frontend dashboard that consumes these endpoints and renders the analytical results as interactive visualisations for Business Owner users.

# 7.7 AI Chatbot Subsystem — TalentTree Multi-Agent Platform

## **7.7.1** **Introduction**

The TalentTree AI Chatbot Subsystem is a stateful, multi-agent platform designed to serve as the AI core of the TalentTree marketplace. Rather than relying on a single generalist model, the system employs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of seven specialized agents — covering brand identity, marketing, copywriting, pricing, logo generation, and general assistance — delivering higher domain-specific quality through a unified conversational interface.

Built for MENA-region SME owners, the platform supports Arabic and English with automatic language detection, regional dialect adaptation, and live competitor-based pricing powered by real-time web search. The subsystem follows a five-layer architecture — Presentation, Application, Orchestration, Agent, and Data — enabling each component to be independently extended or scaled.

## **7.7.2** **System Architecture**

The system runs as a single Python process served by Uvicorn (ASGI), with FastAPI acting as the application framework. FastAPI handles the REST API surface and also hosts the Gradio interactive UI as a mounted sub-application at the root path — all on one port (default 7860). Figure 7.7.1 shows the five-layer architecture, from the presentation tier through to the data and external API services. 

*Figure 7.7.1— TalentTree AI Chatbot: Five-layer system architecture showing presentation, application, orchestration, agent, and            data infrastructure tiers.* 

### **7.7.2.1 Dual Interface Design**

Two access surfaces run in parallel. The Gradio UI, at the root path (`/`), provides four tabs: multi-agent chat, a logo studio (prompt enhancement \+ image generation), a pricing intelligence form, and a read-only catalog viewer. The FastAPI REST endpoint, `POST /api/chat`, accepts seller metadata and a user message as JSON and returns the agent's response as JSON — enabling both direct human use and integration with external or mobile clients.

## **7.7.4 LangGraph Orchestration Engine**

The orchestration layer uses LangGraph's `StateGraph` API, which compiles a declarative graph of nodes and conditional edges into an executable Python callable. Each node receives a shared `AgentState` object, performs its computation, and returns updated state fields. The graph is compiled once at startup and reused across all requests.

### **7.7.4.1 Shared State Schema**

All nodes communicate exclusively through `AgentState`, a 12-field Python `TypedDict` that acts as the system's data bus. Table 5.2 lists its key fields.

  *Table 7.7.2 — Complete AgentState TypedDict schema: the shared data bus across all 7 LangGraph nodes.* 

Listing 7.7.1 presents the complete Python definition of the `AgentState` schema as implemented in `orchestrator/state.py`. 

### *Listing 7.7.1 — AgentState TypedDict definition (orchestrator/state.py): the 12-field shared data bus.* 

### **7.7.4.2  Execution Flow**

*Figure 7.7.3 — LangGraph compiled StateGraph execution flow: every query traverses load\_context → cache\_checker → router → one specialized agent → save\_state → END.* 

### **7.7.4.3 Orchestrator Design Pattern**

*Figure 7.7.4— Orchestrator Design Pattern as implemented in TalentTree. The central LangGraph Orchestrator Agent receives every request from the FastAPI layer, loads session memory, classifies intent, dispatches to one of six specialist workers, invokes external tools where needed, then persists results through the Redis and SQL Server infrastructure layers. The LLM Factory and Pydantic Settings modules provide shared configuration across all components.* 

## **7.7.5 Intelligent Routing Mechanism**

The `orchestrator_router_node` implements a two-tier classification strategy to determine the appropriate specialized agent for each query. The first tier applies deterministic keyword interception before any LLM call is made, providing zero-latency routing for high-confidence intent patterns (logo generation and pricing keywords in both Arabic and English). The second tier invokes the lightweight llama-3.1-8b-instant model (temperature 0.1, max 120 tokens) to classify ambiguous queries into one of seven predefined categories. The router prompt is structured to elicit a single classification keyword with no additional text. Listing 7.7.2 presents the core routing logic. 

*Listing 7.7.2 — orchestrator\_router\_node (orchestrator/router.py): two-tier routing with keyword intercept and LLM fallback* 

*classification.* 

## **7.7.6 Specialized Agent Nodes**

Seven specialized nodes each own a single business domain. Text-generating agents share a common pattern: pull relevant context from `AgentState`, detect language via Arabic Unicode range check, build a domain-specific system prompt, and invoke the appropriate Groq model. Table 7.7.3 summarizes each agent.

Table 7.7.3 — Specialized Agent Node Specifications

*Table 7.7.3 — Complete specification of all seven agent nodes, their LLM configurations, and primary business capabilities.* 

## 

## **7.7.7 Pricing Intelligence Pipeline**

The Pricing agent implements a four-stage internal pipeline that transforms a raw pricing query into a market-driven recommendation grounded in real competitor data. This design departs from conventional LLM chatbots by treating pricing as an active research task rather than a static knowledge retrieval task. Figure 7.7.5 illustrates the four stages. 

*Figure 7.7.5 — Pricing Intelligence Agent: four-stage pipeline from market detection through live web search to market-driven pricing recommendation.*

A key design principle of the pricing agent is that it explicitly rejects static cost-multiplier formulas (e.g., 2× or 4× production cost). All recommendations are grounded exclusively in the current competitor price ranges extracted from live web search results. If the user specifies costs in a different currency from the detected target market, the agent generates an additional exchange rate search query and documents the currency conversion in the output. 

*Table 7.7.4— Three-tier web search provider cascade. Results cached in Redis for 24 hours to minimize API costs on repeated queries.*

### **7.7.9.2 Redis Memory Architecture**

Redis serves two roles: active LLM context memory and a two-level response cache. For context memory, each session's chat history is stored as a Redis List with a maximum depth of 20 messages, trimmed via `ltrim` on every write. The context loader reconstructs the last 10 messages for injection into the next LLM call. Table 7.7.7 documents the complete Redis key schema.

Table 5.7 — Redis Key Schema and Data Types 

*Table 7.7.7 — Redis key schema. System falls back to in-memory Python dict automatically if Redis is unreachable.* 

### 

### **7.7.9.3 Dual-Write Persistence Pattern**

The `save_state_node` implements a dual-write pattern that simultaneously persists every conversation turn to both Redis (for speed) and SQL Server (for durability). For logo generation turns, the node strips the base64 image payload from the Redis write (replacing it with `[Generated Logo Image]`) to prevent context window overflow in subsequent LLM calls. Figure 7.7.6 illustrates the dual-write flow.

*Figure 7.7.6 — Dual-write persistence pattern: save\_state\_node simultaneously writes to Redis (hot path) and SQL Server*   
*(durable trail). Reads prefer Redis, fall back to SQL.* 

Listing 7.7.3 presents the core logic of the `save_chat_message` function that implements   
the dual-write pattern in `repositories/message_repository.py`. 

## **7.7.10 Caching Strategy**

The system implements a two-level response cache in Redis to minimize LLM API call costs and reduce response latency for repeated or semantically similar queries. Table 7.7.8 documents both cache levels.

Table 7.7.8 — Two-Level Response Caching Strategy 

*Table 7.7.8 — Two-level caching: cache writes occur on every turn; reads are bypassed in current configuration by design decision.*

## **7.7.11 Geolocation and Multilingual Support**

Geographic context is detected through a two-layer mechanism. The primary layer performs IP-based geolocation: the client IP is extracted from the `X-Forwarded-For` header, local IPs are resolved to public IPs via `ipify.org`, and country and currency are resolved via `ip-api.com`. The secondary layer performs keyword-based text detection directly from the query, using bilingual keyword lists for all supported MENA markets. This second layer takes priority in the pricing agent, allowing users to query about a target market different from their physical location. Table 7.7.9 documents all supported markets. 

Table 7.7.9 — Supported Geographic Markets and Currency Codes   
**![][image59]**  
*Table 7.7.9 — Twelve supported geographic markets with ISO codes, currency codes, and bilingual keyword detection patterns.*  
   
For multilingual response generation, every agent applies the same Unicode-range language detection: if any character falls within Arabic script range (U+0600–U+06FF), the system prompt includes a rule enforcing formal Modern Standard Arabic (العربية الفصحى); otherwise, English is enforced. The copywriting agent additionally adapts to country-specific Arabic dialect based on the detected location context.

**7.7.15 Chapter Summary**

This chapter presented the architecture and design rationale of the TalentTree AI Chatbot Subsystem — a stateful, multi-agent platform for MENA-region SME owners. Its core innovation is a compiled LangGraph StateGraph that routes each query to one of seven specialized agents rather than relying on a single generalist model, backed by a dual LLM tier strategy, a four-model image generation cascade, a four-stage competitor pricing pipeline, and a dual-write Redis/SQL Server persistence pattern with bilingual, twelve-market support.

The system shows how modern orchestration frameworks (LangGraph), low-latency LLM providers (Groq), and multi-modal image generation (HuggingFace) can be composed into a cohesive platform delivering domain-specialized AI assistance through both a browser interface and a REST API — positioning it for extensibility as new agents are added to the broader TalentTree marketplace.

 **7.8 AI Help Center Chatbot**

This chapter presents the design, implementation, and deployment of the AI-powered Help Center Chatbot developed as part of the Talentree platform. The chatbot — named Tali — serves as the primary point of contact for users seeking guidance on how to navigate and use the Talentree website. It is built on a large language model (LLM) accessed via the HuggingFace Inference API, wrapped in a FastAPI backend, and deployed globally on HuggingFace Spaces using Docker containerization.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

**7.8.1 Introduction** 

As Talentree grows its user base of local entrepreneurs and small brand owners — many of whom are first-time digital platform users — there is a clear need for immediate, accessible support. Traditional support channels such as email or phone introduce response delays that can frustrate new users during their onboarding journey. An AI-powered Help Center chatbot addresses this by providing instant, accurate, and consistent answers around the clock.

The chatbot is intentionally scoped as a navigation and guidance tool only. It does not perform tasks such as writing captions, generating marketing plans, or pricing products — these responsibilities belong to Talentree's dedicated AI feature tools. Tali's role is to direct users to the right tool, explain what each feature does, and ensure users feel supported throughout their journey on the platform.

**7.8.2 System Architecture**

The chatbot system is composed of three main layers: a language model layer hosted on HuggingFace, a backend API layer built with FastAPI, and a frontend integration layer embedded in the Talentree website. Figure 7.8.1 illustrates the complete system architecture and the flow of data between each component.

*Figure 7.8.1 — End-to-end system architecture of the Talentree AI Help Center Chatbot showing the three-layer design: Frontend, Backend API, and AI Model.*

**7.8.4 Model Selection and Rationale** 

Model selection was driven by two primary constraints: instruction-following reliability and zero cost of inference. The system requires a model that can strictly adhere to behavioral rules defined in a system prompt — refusing out-of-scope requests, redirecting task requests to platform tools, and maintaining a warm conversational tone — without inventing information not present in the knowledge base.

Two candidate models were evaluated during development. Table 7.8.2 summarizes the comparison between the initially selected model and the final production model.

**7.8.5 System Prompt and Knowledge Base Design**

The system prompt is the most critical component of the chatbot implementation. It is prepended to every API call as a hidden instruction set that defines the model's identity, behavioral boundaries, knowledge base, and response format. Unlike traditional rule-based chatbots, the LLM interprets these instructions contextually, allowing for nuanced and natural conversations within the defined scope.

**7.8.6.2 Request and Response Format**

The POST /chat endpoint accepts a JSON body containing a list of message objects. Each message has a role field (either "user" or "assistant") and a content field containing the message text. The API is stateless — no session data is stored server-side. The frontend is responsible for maintaining and sending the complete conversation history with every request, enabling the model to preserve conversational context across multiple turns.

Listing 7.8.1 shows an example multi-turn request body demonstrating how the frontend sends conversation history to maintain context across multiple exchanges.

*Listing 7.8.1 — Multi-turn POST /chat request body showing conversation history with alternating user and assistant roles.*

string. Listing 7.8.2 shows the corresponding response object for the above request. 

*Listing 7.8.2 — POST /chat success response containing the bot's reply string.* 

**7.8.6.3 Backend Implementation**

**7.8.9.1 Deployment Architecture**

The chatbot API is deployed as a Docker-based application on HuggingFace Spaces — a free cloud hosting platform that provides HTTPS access, automatic container orchestration, and global availability. The deployment pipeline is fully automated: any push to the HuggingFace Space repository triggers a rebuild and redeployment of the container.

**7.8.10 Frontend Integration**

The chatbot API is designed to be framework-agnostic. The frontend team integrates it using a JavaScript function that manages conversation history locally and sends the complete history with each request. The API requires no authentication token from the client side — all model authentication is handled server-side using a HuggingFace token stored as a container secret.

**7.8.12 Chapter Summary**

This chapter presented the complete design, implementation, and deployment of the Talentree AI Help Center Chatbot. The system leverages Meta's Llama 3.1 8B Instruct language model — accessed via the HuggingFace Inference API — to provide natural, contextually appropriate responses to user queries about the Talentree platform.

The chatbot's behavioral architecture is governed entirely by a carefully engineered system prompt that enforces strict scope boundaries, prevents hallucination through multiple complementary measures, and maintains a warm and encouraging conversational tone. The system correctly handles four categories of user input: direct platform questions, tool redirection requests, off-topic refusals, and unknown-answer fallbacks.

The API is deployed at zero cost on HuggingFace Spaces using Docker containerization, providing a globally accessible HTTPS endpoint. The frontend integration requires no third-party libraries — only the browser's native fetch API and a conversation history array managed in client memory. All security-sensitive credentials are managed server-side and never exposed to the client.

# **CHAPTER 8: Testing & Validation**

---

## 8.1 Introduction
The integration of a multi-vendor digital marketplace and business growth engine requires a defensive, high-coverage validation phase to guarantee structural reliability and user workflow safety. This chapter details the comprehensive testing methodology implemented across the Talentree platform. The primary objective is to verify that the modular Angular user interfaces, the decoupled ASP.NET Core 8.0 Onion Architecture backend, and the continuous Python FastAPI machine learning pipelines collaborate seamlessly without fracturing core transaction constraints. Validation encompasses an intentional balance between rigorous developer-led exploration, automated API verification, and systematic model lifecycle monitoring.

## 8.2 Testing Strategy and Environment
The core architectural layers of the platform were evaluated inside a synchronized staging environment built to emulate modern production deployment configurations. This baseline environment setup mitigates hardware performance variance and ensures that system response velocities reflect realistic load parameters. 

The underlying infrastructure includes high-compute host machines synced with local SQL Server instances and stateful Redis clusters. Rather than testing components in isolation, the runtime environment bridges frontend single-page modules with backend routing controllers to evaluate data consistency as objects cross network boundaries.

### 8.2.1 Manual UI & Usability Testing
Manual exploration served as the absolute validation boundary for user experience assessment, structural navigation correctness, and cross-device interface scaling. The frontend development sub-team executed end-to-end execution scenarios across diverse mobile, tablet, and desktop browser viewports spanning from three hundred and twenty pixels up to twenty-five hundred and sixty pixels in width. These evaluations verified form entry behaviors, state-driven loading representations, and instantaneous validation responses across the Customer, Business Owner, and Administration micro-portals.

### 8.2.2 Browser Developer Tools and Network Tab Integration
During full-platform manual execution, Google Chrome Developer Tools (Chrome DevTools) provided continuous runtime diagnostics. The development teams utilized the Network tab to intercept out-bound HTTP serialization requests, confirming payload completeness and assuring that core transactional endpoints respond safely below the mandatory five hundred millisecond threshold. Furthermore, the Network tab was instrumental in auditing persistent WebSocket data streams managed by the SignalR NotificationHub, verifying binary frame delivery intervals. Simultaneously, the Application storage tab was used to review active cookie parameters and local storage partitions to confirm that cryptographic JWT elements are safely held and isolated based on user authorization claims.

## 8.3 Automated API Verification (Postman)
The backend service surface, encapsulating over eighty distinct RESTful endpoints, was protected via a centralized Postman Workspace. The engineering team organized this workspace into individual Collections categorized strictly by domain responsibility, such as Authentication, Production Operations, Payout ledgers, and Supplier Material procurement. 

### 8.3.1 Dynamic Token Extraction Scripts
To optimize workflow velocity, the collection root incorporates automated Post-response evaluation scripts. Upon a successful login or profile registration execution, the automated post-test script parses the incoming JSON data structure, extracts the freshly minted access token parameter, and maps it directly into a dynamic environment variable. Every nested resource folder inherits this security token configuration, dynamically prepending the bearer asset into the standard HTTP Authorization headers, allowing continuous, frictionless execution of secure platform capabilities.

### 8.3.2 Global Exception Middleware and Schema Standardization
API validation confirmed that the backend Global Exception Handling Middleware properly captures unhandled domain faults, transforming them into a standardized API response model. Tests executed against malformed checkout coordinates or invalid payment identifiers proved that the pipeline successfully suppresses low-level server stack details, mapping raw exceptions into safe, uniform JSON error models carrying proper HTTP status codes.

### 8.3.3 Stripe Webhook Signature Protection
Specialized integration test collections targeted the payment route. Because the Stripe webhook callback endpoint must remain accessible from the public internet, testing confirmed that the system utilizes signature verification logic. Incoming requests lacking a valid cryptographic signature token are dropped instantly at the gateway level, returning bad request responses to protect against request spoofing and external injection attempts.

## 8.4 Infrastructure and Integration Validation
Integration verification proved that the system layers preserve data states as transactions navigate through independent runtime subsystems.

### 8.4.1 Entity Framework Core Tracking and Interception
The integration layer verified the correct lifecycle management of persistent database models within the data access boundaries:
* **Audit Tracking Interception:** Tests proved that entity creation automatically invokes the internal AuditInterceptor, populating creation timestamps and author identities, while updates correctly preserve historical metrics.
* **Global Soft-Delete Query Filtering:** Validation confirmed that executing an inventory or product removal command flips the logical delete flag to true without breaking database row durability. Subsequent LINQ queries automatically incorporate dynamic query filters to bypass logically deleted elements.

### 8.4.2 SignalR WebSocket Connectivity
Integration testing confirmed the stability of the bidirectional messaging channel. Upon connection, users are dynamically isolated into dedicated notification groups. Testing confirmed that triggering a status change—such as an administrator approving a manufacturing quote—instantly transmits an operational message envelope to the target client within ten milliseconds, operating over a safe fifteen-second keep-alive ping loop.

## 8.5 Machine Learning & AI Pipeline Validation

### 8.5.1 Automated Model Retraining and Optimization via MLflow
To eliminate unmonitored mathematical decay or statistical version mismatch within the Python-based AI analytics microservice, the architecture incorporates an MLflow tracking pipeline. When background RabbitMQ consumers detect fresh platform datasets, an automated retraining sequence is executed. 

The engine writes candidate parameters directly to MLflow, which systematically calculates, plots, and compares accuracy statistics and Mean Absolute Error attributes against the existing production candidate. The tracking server visualizes performance metrics and dynamically applies the active Production tag to the highest-scoring model while archiving older versions. The FastAPI layer automatically queries this production reference tag to serve optimized calculations to the dashboard interfaces.

## 8.6 Non-Functional Verification Matrix
System operational properties were audited under simulated load conditions to confirm overall platform health. Validation verified that the token authentication mechanism performs with negligible processing delay. The cryptographic webhook checks successfully drop altered payloads while maintaining data safety. Parameterized query abstractions embedded inside core specifications proved to completely neutralize SQL injection vulnerabilities, as confirmed by inspecting generated database query logs. Finally, multimedia management validation proved that transforming raw filenames into structured GUID identifiers completely blocks directory traversal exploits and asset collision hazards.

# **CHAPTER 9: Conclusion & Future Work**

This closing chapter summarizes what the Talentree platform set out to achieve, reflects on how the delivered MVP addresses those goals, acknowledges the limitations accepted for this release, and outlines the roadmap of features planned for future phases.

9.1 Project Summary

Talentree is a digital marketplace platform built to empower small businesses and independent creators in three focused categories — Fashion & Accessories, Handmade Crafts, and Natural & Beauty Products — by giving them a single place to sell finished products, source raw materials, and grow their business with the help of AI. The system was delivered as three cooperating subsystems: an Angular single-page frontend, an ASP.NET Core Web API handling business logic and data persistence, and a set of Python-based AI microservices providing recommendations, insights, and conversational assistance. Three user roles — Customer, Business Owner, and Administrator (with a Super Administrator tier) — were supported end-to-end, from registration and approval workflows through browsing, ordering, secure Stripe payments, and platform moderation.

![][image61]9.2 Achievements

Table 9.1 maps the primary goals set out for the MVP against how the delivered platform addresses each one.

**Table 9.1 — MVP Goals vs. Delivered Outcomes**

**![][image62]**

9.3 Limitations of the Current System

To keep the MVP achievable within the project timeline, several features were deliberately scoped out of this release:

* No direct messaging between buyers and sellers — communication is currently limited to reviews and support tickets.  
* No native mobile applications (iOS/Android); the platform is web-only and responsive from 320px to 2560px.  
* No multi-language support — the interface is English-only, with Arabic deferred.  
* Payment is limited to Stripe; local Egyptian gateways (Paymob, Fawry) are not yet integrated.  
* No loyalty, referral, or premium-subscription programs.  
* Analytics are descriptive rather than predictive — no forecasting or fraud-detection models are included yet.
